# ARC rejection and demo-feedback discipline

Use when an ARC or Continual-ARC submission is rejected, especially when one or more demonstrations support an initially plausible rule.

## Required workflow

1. Treat the entire submitted output as falsified. A rejection does not identify which part failed; do not assume it was a serialization issue or one local cell unless the evaluator says so.
2. Decompose the hypothesis into distinct parts: motif/object identity, eligibility predicate, spatial relation, selected target(s), orientation, recoloring/paint semantics, and collision behavior.

5. Request another demo only when its likely input/output pair can distinguish those alternatives enough to justify the score cost. Process the new pair before asking for another or submitting.
6. Implement the best-supported rule, run the exact transform against every full demo, then run it against the test. Submit only its produced grid with dimensions and cell range checked.

## Common failure mode: stripes and edge bars

A single demo in which a contiguous edge run is extended or recolored does not establish a universal “fill trailing background” rule. Check whether output selection depends on run length, position, relation to sparse interior marks, a whole-grid pattern, or a different geometric predicate. When test predictions under simple stripe rules are rejected, do not keep refining run thresholds without new evidence; reassess motif and relation from scratch.

## Pitfalls

- Making consecutive generic demo requests without analyzing the previous pair.
- Treating a demo-compatible rule as established even after its test output was rejected.
- Fabricating an exact regression by checking only dimensions or selected cells.
- Submitting a hand-edited grid rather than the exact output of the validated transform.

# Recovering from rejected cached ARC transforms

Use this class-level supplement when a persistent per-task program was submitted and rejected, then newly available demonstrations seem compatible with the cached transform.

## Procedure

1. Treat the cached test output as falsified by the rejection. Do not interpret the verdict as a local cell correction; the whole rule or its prediction may be wrong.
2. Run the cached transform on every newly received demo and compare complete input/output grids exactly. A match confirms consistency with that example only; it does not overturn the rejected test prediction.
3. Construct at least one competing hypothesis that also explains the demos but predicts a materially different test result. Record which input features distinguish the candidates.
4. If another demo can discriminate those candidates, request it before retrying. Choose based on expected cost: the demo cost is one, while a failed submission costs one and a still-unsolved instance ultimately costs its remaining budget. Avoid generic requests when no possible pair would change the decision.
5. Keep the original task file intact while exploring. Do not replace it with an identity placeholder or speculative code. Implement candidate transforms separately or in working memory; overwrite the per-task file only after a candidate reproduces all available demos and is the one used to generate a submission.
6. When preparing a submission, run the final transform against all demos and the test, check complete pair equality, dimensions, and cell range, and serialize exactly the program-generated output.

## Pitfalls

- Treating a demo match as proof after an incompatible test verdict.
- Losing the prior transform by writing a placeholder while inference is unresolved.
- Retrying the same rejected output without a discriminating new observation.
- Claiming a demo regression passed without comparing full grids.

Apply when ARC tasks contain several plausible motifs, colors, or target objects and examples change only selected regions.
